analysis.one_liner: Keeps most medical debt off credit reports and requires notice before reporting it.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with no cosponsors, never received a committee vote or floor action before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Fair Credit Reporting Act so that credit bureaus cannot put medical debt on a credit report unless it has been in collections for at least a year, and they could never report medical debt that was paid or settled within that year. It would also require anyone reporting medical debt to first notify the person and give them a detailed accounting of the debt. It was introduced on October 6, 2020 and referred to the House Financial Services Committee, where it stayed until the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.who_benefits: People whose medical bills would otherwise show up on their credit reports, usually patients who were billed unexpectedly or disputed a charge while the hospital sold or assigned the debt to a collector. Medical bills are a leading cause of damaged credit even for people who eventually pay; keeping uncollected and recently placed debt off reports protects credit scores that determine access to loans, apartments, and jobs.

how_it_helps.text: Credit bureaus could not report medical debt that has not been placed for collection, charged to profit or loss, or subjected to a similar action [S2][S3].
They also could not report medical debt placed for collection less than a year before the report, or debt fully paid or settled within that one-year window [S2][S3].

Before furnishing medical debt information to a credit bureau, a person must notify the consumer of these reporting restrictions and ensure the consumer receives a detailed accounting of the debt [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Credit reporting agencies, debt collectors, and health care providers would lose a tool they use to pressure patients: the threat that an unpaid medical bill will appear on a credit report and damage their credit score. Lenders would also lose information about medical debts that are less than a year old.
analysis.who_pays_short: Credit bureaus, debt collectors, health providers

drawbacks.text: Restricting what credit bureaus can report removes information lenders use to price credit; lenders could respond by charging everyone slightly more or lending less, a cost borne broadly rather than by the patients the bill protects [S2][S3].

The bill changes reporting, not the underlying debt: people would still owe the medical bills, and hospitals and collectors could still pursue payment through lawsuits, liens, and collection calls; only the credit-report lever would be delayed or blocked [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit is real and targeted: it would shield millions of people from credit-score damage from bills they did not expect, did not incur, or paid quickly. The costs are real but modest and diffuse — slightly less information for lenders and no reduction in the underlying debt itself. On balance the protections for patients outweigh the costs to the reporting and collection industries, though the bill would have been stronger if it also addressed why medical bills arise.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 116th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Mike Gallagher introduced the Fair Medical Debt Reporting Act on October 6, 2020 [S1][S2].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services on the day it was introduced [S5].
No further action was taken before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit bureaus, medical debt collectors, and providers kept the ability to put medical bills on credit reports. People with medical debt got no relief, and the bill expired without a cosponsor or a hearing.

for.name: Mike Gallagher
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, which would keep most medical debt off credit reports

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; never scheduled action on the bill
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on October 6, 2020 and took no action — no hearing, markup, or report — before the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: No votes or recorded opposition exist; the bill had a single Republican sponsor and no cosponsors of either party before it expired.

industries.note: The bill would bar Experian, Equifax, and TransUnion from reporting most medical debt, shrinking the data they sell to lenders. Keeping medical bills on reports lets bureaus sell a record of patients' misfortunes; its removal benefits consumers' credit scores.

Collectors lose the credit-report threat for their first year of collection and for debts paid quickly, a key lever for pressuring patients to pay. Their business model depends on converting billed patients into paying customers under that pressure.

Hospitals and other providers lose a collection tool for unpaid bills, since patients would face less credit damage in the first year and after settling. They could still sue or refer debt to collectors, but with one less source of leverage.
